blocks.title: Dimensions
blocks.text: Any physical quantity can be described by certain familiar properties such as length, mass, time, temperature and electric current; these measurable properties are called dimensions. Dimensions deal with the qualitative nature of a physical quantity in terms of the fundamental quantities. Quantities such as length, depth, height, diameter and light year are all measured in metres and denoted by the same dimension, length, given the symbol L written within square brackets, [L]. Similarly mass, time, electric current and temperature are denoted by [M], [T], [A] and [theta]. These five dimensions have been chosen as basic because they are easy to measure in experiments.

The dimensions of other quantities indicate how they are related to the basic quantities and are combinations of the fundamental dimensions. Speed v is measured in metres per second, so it has the dimensions of length divided by time: [v] = [L]/[T] = [L][T^-1] = [LT^-1]. As acceleration a = delta v / delta t, [a] = [v]/[T] = [LT^-1]/[T] = [LT^-2]. Also the dimensions of force can be written as [F] = [m][a] = [M][LT^-2] = [MLT^-2]. By the use of dimensionality we can check the homogeneity (correctness) of a physical equation, and also derive a formula for a physical quantity.

The correctness of an equation can be checked by showing that the dimensions of the quantities on both sides of the equation are the same; this is the principle of homogeneity. Suppose a car starts from rest (v_i = 0) and covers a distance S in time t moving with acceleration a. The equation of motion is S = v_i t + (1/2) a t^2, or S = (1/2) a t^2. Numerical factors like 1/2 have no dimensions, so they can be ignored. Putting the dimensions of both sides: [S] = [a][t^2]; writing the symbols of dimensions, [L] = [LT^-2][T^2] = [LT^-2 T^2], or [L] = [L]. The dimensions on both sides are the same, therefore the equation is dimensionally correct.
Dimensionality can be used to derive a possible formula for a physical quantity by correct estimation of the various factors on which the quantity depends.

blocks.title: Example 1.4
blocks.text: Derive a formula for the centripetal force required to keep an object moving along a circle with uniform speed, assuming that the centripetal force depends on the mass of the object, the radius of the circle and the uniform speed. Solution: as the force depends on the mass m, the radius r and the uniform speed v, F is proportional to m^a v^b r^c, so F = (constant) m^a v^b r^c ... (i), where the exponents a, b and c are to be determined. By the principle of homogeneity the dimensions on both sides must be the same; the constant has no dimension, so ignoring it: [F] = [m^a][v^b][r^c], [MLT^-2] = [M^a][L/T]^b[L]^c = [M^a][LT^-1]^b[L]^c, [MLT^-2] = [M^a L^(b+c) T^-b] ... (ii). Comparing the powers of the dimensions on both sides: a = 1; b + c = 1; -b = -2. Solving, a = 1, b = 2, c = -1. Putting these values in equation (i): F = (constant) m v^2 r^-1, or F = (constant) m v^2 / r. The numerical value of the constant cannot be determined by dimensional analysis; it can be found by experiment, and here it happens to be 1, so the equation reduces to F = m v^2 / r.

The dimensional method cannot identify where an equation is wrong. Even if an equation is proved correct, we can only say the equation might be correct, because the method does not provide a check on any numerical factor or constant; that can only be determined by experiments or by plotting some suitable graph between the variables.

blocks.text: Side boxes: the caesium atomic frequency standard at the National Institute of Standards and Technology in Colorado (USA) is the primary standard for the unit of time; the escapement, an anchor with pallets engaging an escape wheel and regulated by a pendulum, is the device that made the pendulum clock practical; a scale of specific temperatures runs from the outer part of the Sun (about 6000 degrees C) through a lamp filament, a roaring Bunsen flame, melting aluminium and boiling mercury to boiling water (100 degrees C), melting ice (0 degrees C), freezing alcohol, liquefying air and absolute zero (-273 degrees C); and calculators yield as many digits as their memory permits, so final answers must be rounded to the correct number of significant figures (Beware).

blocks.prompt: Check whether v^2 = v_i^2 + 2 a S is dimensionally correct, and show by dimensions that the period of a simple pendulum T depends on l and g as T = constant x sqrt(l/g) (numerical problem 1.8).
blocks.explanation: [v^2] = [LT^-1]^2 = [L^2 T^-2]; [v_i^2] is the same, and [a S] = [LT^-2][L] = [L^2 T^-2], so every term has the dimensions [L^2 T^-2] and the equation is homogeneous. For the pendulum, let T = (constant) l^a g^b: [T] = [L]^a [LT^-2]^b = [L^(a+b) T^-2b], so a + b = 0 and -2b = 1, giving b = -1/2 and a = 1/2; hence T = constant x l^(1/2) g^(-1/2) = constant x sqrt(l/g). The constant (2 pi) cannot come from dimensions.

items: Dimensions: [L], [M], [T], [A], [theta]; [v] = [LT^-1], [a] = [LT^-2], [F] = [MLT^-2]. Homogeneity: both sides of a correct equation have the same dimensions (S = 1/2 a t^2 gives [L] = [L]); numerical factors have no dimensions.
Derivation: F = (constant) m^a v^b r^c, matching powers gives a = 1, b = 2, c = -1, so F = m v^2 / r (constant 1 by experiment). Limitation: no check on constants or on where an equation is wrong.
